I got some old pins that came from a shearing shed that was moved to a winery and converted into a restaurant. Sadly, the winery and restaurant burned down in a bush fire a couple of years ago. The original shed was build around 1900 from what I remember.

Decided the pins felt nice in the hand, so I made a bottle opener from one of them.

Pretty simple, and rustic, smithing.

Used a gas forge that I built from a kit and an old gas cylinder:

...the fuck did you do to that anvil? Is that a HF cast iron anvil? Dude, do yourself a favor and cruise craigslist for a chunk of railroad track is nothing else. It will save you three quarters of the work. It may not seem like a lot now, but your elbow and shoulder will thank you in ten years.

I don't know what your skill level is, so I can't comment on the work. I've been working metal for a little over twenty years, and judging by your comment about getting a forge up and running, I take it you are fairly new to it. Drifting metal like that isn't really easy, so you have either talent or a big scrap pile.

Invest in quality tools even if it means fewer, wear hearing/eye/lung protection religiously, and make damned sure you practice proper form. It really sucks to grow to enjoy something like this only to tear your body up to the point where you can't enjoy it anymore.

It's actually a nice anvil, swedish made in 1921. It's a 121lb anvil with a forged steel face. The dings in it can sometimes leave marks in my work, but I typically make rustic looking stuff anyway, so the odd mark doesn't matter too much to me.

I didn't inflict the scars it has, that's just what happens to anvils that spend most of their lives on a farm. It's been hit with an angle grinder a few times over the years. Overall, it's in reasonable condition, the top is nice and flat.

Most of the tools I used to make this were home made. Made a slitting punch from some old spring, some drifts to open it up from various bits and pieces and a ball punch to make the little tab thingy from some really hard rod that happened to already have a spherical end on it.

I'd definitely class myself as a beginner/novice, I've done a couple of short courses a few years ago, so I'm ok with some of the basics, even a little forge welding. Definitely no master though. I have a nice (bought new) German 1.2kg hammer and collect/make tools as I need them and as time permits. I also have a 5" post vise that was originally my great grandfathers.
